column1: Copper demand, Chinese factories and money
column3: Copper is wired into industry, so a firm copper-to-gold ratio tends to come with busy factories. (The link to US money supply is weak, so that leg is no longer counted.) — the copper price vs gold: rising · Chinese factory activity: rising
Gold and oil are priced in US dollars, so a strong dollar tends to weigh on them, and a weak one tends to lift them. — the dollar: rising · gold: falling · oil: rising

column1: The RBA rate, home loans and household debt
column3: When the RBA changes the cash rate, the home-loan rates people actually pay tend to follow one to three months later; the card reads pass-through pending until that data exists. (The debt leg is a debt-to-income level, not a debt-servicing cost.) — the RBA cash rate: rising · the home-loan rate people pay: steady · household debt ratios: rising

column1: Oil, inflation expectations and borrowing costs
column3: When oil jumps, markets tend to expect more inflation, and long-term borrowing costs tend to rise with it. — oil: rising · inflation expectations: falling · 10-year borrowing costs: rising

column1: Iron ore, the terms of trade and the Australian dollar
column3: Iron ore is one of Australia’s biggest exports, so firm export prices tend to lift the terms of trade and, over time, the Australian dollar. The US dollar rides along as context: a falling Australian dollar is often mostly a rising US dollar. — iron ore: rising · the terms of trade: falling · the Australian dollar: falling · the US dollar: rising
